title: HRV: What Your Nervous System Is Actually Telling You
description: A working explanation of heart rate variability — what the number represents, why comparing it to other people is meaningless, and how to use a seven-day trend instead of a daily score.
takeaways: HRV is a measure of autonomic balance, not a fitness score. Absolute values are not comparable between people.
Alcohol is the most reliable single suppressor of HRV, with visible effects for one to two nights.
A three-day sustained drop against your baseline is information; a one-day drop is noise.
Slow-paced breathing at six breaths per minute raises HRV measurably within a single session.

title: Sleep Architecture and Longevity
answers: Why does sleep quality affect how fast we age?
description: Why deep sleep is front-loaded into the first half of the night, what the glymphatic system does while you are in it, and why sleep consistency may matter more than sleep duration.
takeaways: Deep sleep concentrates in the first half of the night, so a late bedtime cuts it disproportionately.
Glymphatic clearance of metabolic waste from the brain increases substantially during slow-wave sleep.
Sleep timing consistency predicts health outcomes independently of total sleep duration.
Loud snoring or unrefreshing sleep after adequate hours warrants a clinical assessment, not another supplement.

title: The NAD+ Question: Separating Mechanism From Marketing
description: An honest look at what NAD+ precursor trials have shown in humans, why mouse results have not translated, and which non-supplement levers raise NAD+ for free.
takeaways: NAD+ decline with age is well documented. Whether oral precursors restore tissue function is the open question.
Human trials reliably show raised blood NAD+ but inconsistent functional outcomes.
Exercise, energy restriction and reduced alcohol all raise NAD+ without a supplement.
No head-to-head human data establishes NMN as superior to NR or niacin.

title: Fix Metabolic Health Before You Chase Longevity
answers: Which blood markers matter most for metabolic health?
description: Why fasting insulin is the marker most annual checkups leave out, how ApoB reframes cardiovascular risk, and what a two-week CGM experiment can and cannot teach you.
takeaways: Fasting insulin rises years before fasting glucose does, making it the earlier warning signal.
ApoB counts atherogenic particles; LDL cholesterol measures their contents. The two can disagree.
A CGM is best used as a time-limited learning tool, not a permanent dashboard.
Laboratory reference ranges describe the population, and a large part of that population is metabolically unwell.

title: Heat, Cold and Hormesis: Using Stress on Purpose
answers: Is cold plunging better than sauna?
description: The Finnish cohort data on sauna frequency, the catecholamine response to cold water, and the one timing mistake that undermines strength training.
takeaways: Sauna use four to seven times weekly showed the largest mortality reduction in Finnish cohort data.
Cold water immersion raises noradrenaline by 200 to 300 percent, with effects lasting well past the session.
Cold within a few hours after resistance training blunts hypertrophy signalling.
Contrast protocols finishing with heat in the evening may support sleep onset through core temperature drop.

title: Protein, Muscle and Aging Well
answers: How much protein do older adults need?
description: Anabolic resistance, the leucine threshold, and why the protein restriction argument from longevity research runs into sarcopenia data after age 50.
takeaways: Older muscle is less sensitive to the anabolic signal, so per-meal protein needs rise with age.
Three to four meals of 30 to 40 grams beat the same total concentrated at dinner.
Sarcopenia is one of the strongest predictors of frailty and mortality in older adults.
Periodic energy restriction is a better autophagy lever than chronic protein restriction.

title: Light, the Circadian Clock and Modern Life
answers: How does light affect the body clock?
description: How morning outdoor light sets melatonin onset 14 to 16 hours later, why peripheral clocks respond to meal timing, and what shift work does to metabolism.
takeaways: Outdoor light is many times brighter than indoor lighting and is the dominant circadian signal.
Peripheral clocks in liver, gut and muscle are entrained partly by when you eat.
Most self-described night owls have a reversible delayed phase rather than a fixed chronotype.
Evening overhead lighting is a larger melatonin suppressor than most people assume.

title: How to Read a Study Without Being Fooled
answers: How do I tell good health research from bad?
description: Mouse versus human, surrogate markers versus outcomes, absolute versus relative risk, and the specific claims in biohacking that fail each test.
takeaways: A surrogate marker moving is not the same as an outcome improving — the NAD+ field is the clearest current example.
Rodent metabolic rates are several times higher than human, which breaks most fasting-duration extrapolations.
Relative risk reduction without the absolute numbers is the most common way statistics mislead.
Small, short, unblinded trials with industry funding should shift your confidence, not settle the question.
